Usage: When naiwa combines with another Tanji to form a new kana, it uses the -(n)ata form. If the word is consonant final, such as hon, it forms honata. If the word is vowel final, such as "kangi," it takes the last vowel and replaces it with 'a,' thus forming 'kangata.' If the word is a much smaller CV unit, such as kó or ai, the '-se' form is used, forming aitase or kotase.

oru often connects in the -wu form to radicals. for example, bo+oru -> bwu. for consonant-final radicals, it simply takes the oru form. for radicals ending in approximants or vowel-approximant units, like kowo, it takes the -rou form, so kowo+ru->koworou.
Definitions: own; the sixth of celestial stems

Usage: it often affects labiovelarises the first consonant when appearing in compounds and changes the first and second vowel to -o and -i respectively. In the compound hyogomi, it changes it to hwogimi.
in compounds, the 'are' form is used (hwaregimi).
often simplifies into nki when appearing after nasals.
it open appears in the -w- form and changes the vowel in front of it to an 'a' (e.g., in re+awa+uru+iki (rewaruiki), the uru changes to aru)
is not pronounced with a glottal stop when at the start or end of a radical (e.g., 'a+gyo=hagyo; aiso+'a=aisa; ena+'a=enaha)

when clustering with consonants like gyo+hin, it changes to the /ɪn/ (in) form. so gyo+hin->gyin. has a tendency to depalatalise, especially if '(h)in' is below a velar, such as in 'gyo+hin+iki' = hin+iki=hinki. gyo+hinki=ginki.
often a connective, taking the vowel of the word before and after it

usually aspirates the main consonant, so kowo+orin -> cowarin. The preceding vowel changes to 'a' to harmonise with 'i' in (a)rin. If the word is consonant-final, like hon, then the vowel harmonises with the latest vowel in the word. as for hon, this is 'o,' so o->u to match 'i', becoming honurin.
often takes the previous vowel, so naiwa+eme->naiweme. iki+eme->ikeme. but for smaller units, like bare CV or VV, it does not, so ma+eme->maeme.
often used in compounds denoting semi-solidity or chocolatey or velvety textures, like in 'bunica' (brown chocolate) or 'ohiraca' (milk/white chocolate).

hó broadly refers to tuberous vegetables as hongu. It can also refer to potato seeds (hongo) and specific anatomical parts, like the eyes or the tuber itself (honga). As hóshí, it can refer to the apical bud or the potato seed.
replaces the final vowel of the radical with -u, so rwanka + uta -> rwankuta. If the radical is a small V(N)/CV unit like ka, then it's used as a circumfix (u-tau -> ukatau).

A native Tanji. It is used in all bread-related roots: jireipan (flat-bread (refers to naan)), napisamipan (long-fish-bread (refers to croissants)), etc. Numbers added as suffix denote number (e.g., panzu (sandwich / two breads), pansu (slice / one bread), panwu (clubhouse sandwich), etc.)

a privative prefix, denoting lacking of something. Reduces to the an- form before velars and am- form before bilabials. Example: angchi (dry, arid), angniren (blind), angniro (without eyes / eyeless), angasa (homeless), angmani (poor), angatase (joyless), angfosho (lonely), etc.

Turns a root into a profession of someone / their life. Kamu = eat, kamumasu = eater (e.g., gourmet), but Kamugeo is a professional food critic. Similar to how maooru means defence and maofaru means law-defence. So maofageru would mean lawyer. It can be explicitly professional with dae- (madaefageru) but context often does the work.

im- before bilabials, in- before velars. Refers to the canonical object used for something; e.g., ingshiremai (textbook), impamya (writing apparatus), inkamu (utensils), ingchihai (deglutition muscles), ingikamebang (kitchenware)
the canonical place where something happens; e.g., rawaeba (bedroom), ikamebang (kitchen).

A circumfix. It attaches like: i(root)ng; e.g., ikamung (cook), iasang (build a house), idaming (make easy). o-roots take -eba before i-ng, but normal roots don't: iasangeba (construction site for a home).
A prefix that indicates a group of; e.g., usengoshi (flock of birds), usehon (group of people), etc.

Suffix for entering or into; e.g., riwakangosunje (into my mind / introduction to me), asaje (into the house), asagaje (within the house's walls / intramural). With verbs: shahadajeru (put into battle; embattle), asajeru (put into a home), motojeru (put into a position of strength / empower), manijeru (put into a position of wealth); jijeru (insert). Other types: bakarejei (esoteric; attributive). Naranarejei = narana (mysterious) + re (inner) + je (into) + i (attributive) = insider mystic / esoteric. The 'de' form is used for out of and is an irregular reversive of je: motode (remove from power), naranaredei (exoteric), manideru (to impoverish / make poor), etc. The fact that deru is used for put out of is completely a coincidence (I chose deru before learning 出る).

Means above or over. Is a prefix; e.g., ujasa (roof / above the house), ujosora (space / transcending the sky), ujoriwakango (incomprehensible / above the brain), ujohon (übermensch, transcending humans), ujohonina (megalomaniac), ujomoto (above strength / transcending strength). Ujomoto is extremely strong, if you want to say 'excess of strength,' you might say omoto or if you wanted to say 'superstrength,' you might say momoto or motonyi. Ujoku and ujogu are the figurative and literal forms respectively.

Prefix indicating inferiority; e.g., unkuriwakango (subconscious - figurative lower brain). Unku is used for figurative roots and ungu is used for literal roots; e.g., ungumakurenga (below amygdaloid nucleus).
A suffix, like -sis in English, denoting illness; e.g., angrawaina (insomnia), ujohonina (meglomania), etc.

refers to something besides or near something else; e.g., menapi (parallel), mejioe (adjacent), measa (besides the house), mehon (human-adjacent), meuns (aligned with life). A planet that could harbour life would be meunshi. You can use -ku/-gu to disambiguate literalness but context often does the work. The opposite would be pe (irregular reversive). Peuns (not aligned with life), pehon (not adjacent to humans), pehonhwo (immoral / not aligned with humanity).
Prefix for 'for' or favour; e.g., kohongi (pro-humanity), koumatachi (pro-communism), kangmanigi (pro-postmoney / pro-moneylessness), etc. ko + ang forms kang (pro-X-less).

Used for the concept or idea of something as a suffix; e.g., hongi (humanity), hakugi (reality), unsogi (vitality, life itself). -wi is used for theories or -ologies and -kuwi for intangible extensions of those; e.g., riwakankuwi (psychology), riwakangwi (neuroscience), gayawi (physics), gayakuwi (metaphysics), honwi (anthropology), naiwawi (theory of happiness). For a subjective philosophy, -wi with the proper possessive/genitive is used: unshwisun (my view on life / life philosophy), zhamuwisan (her view on god), Maika no makurewi (Mica's view on inner sobs / trials). -tachi for -isms: hontachi (humanism), umatachi (communitarianism; e.g., communism).
like anti- or retro-; e.g., ocetawa (regression), oceangmanigi (anti-moneylessess), oceumatachi (anti-communism), ocehongi (anti-humanity), ocehontachi (anti-humanism), etc.

A prefix indicating orbit or aroundness. bau- is used for simple orbit or aroundness whereas bam- is used for path or trajectory. Examples with bau-: baubaka (circular orbit), bauitagi (orbiting the idea), bauhon (revolving around humans), bauikamebangtachi (ideology revolving around kitchens), bauhongitachi (ideology revolving around humanity). With -bam: bambaka (circumference), bambaubaka (circumference / trajectory of a circular orbit), bamrwanakden (the train's trajectory), bamkitaginya (the trajectory of this love/relationship / where a relationship is headed)

A prefix, like trans-, inter-, or intra-. Usually refers to 'between one or more;' e.g., genhakashi (interfamilial), genhon (interpersonal), genasa (through homes / between homes), genuns (between lives; e.g., a drug dealer). zon is the limited form; e.g., zonhakashi (within the family), zonasa (within the house), zonuns (within life), zonhon (within people), though -je is recommended instead of zon-: hakashije, unsoje, honje, etc. Zon- is restrictive (emphasis on exclusivity) and -je is about the intoness. For an introduction, you'd use riwakangosunje (into my mind), since it's non-exclusive. For private thoughts, you'd use zonriwakangosun (within my mind / private to my mind). The zom- form is used before bilabials.

refers to the self-; e.g., emononsu (selfie / self-picture), mensujamu (self-alignment with The God / conscience), mensuhon, pensu (self-unalignment / cognitive dissonance), mensu (self-alignment / congruence / cognitive congruence),etc. The standalone form for the self depends: ansu (the self that acts), onsu (the self that experiences), ninsu (the main self / self around which everything revolves), omgsu (the subjugated self / bound self with no control), amgsu (the self that chooses to experience). Hosu is used for 'the person's self' / 'one's oneness.' It literally means "potato-me or one potato," but due to significance of potatoes in Tawish culture, hosu is used for one's oneness / what makes one him.
used like post- in English; e.g., echiangmanigi (post-moneylessness), echiseko (after 6 days; i.e., the weekends). To say 'after the weekends,' you'd use zhinyi (after), like 'zhinyi echiseko.'
